title_card: Why Is It Called Black Friday?

lines.text: It's the day after Thanksgiving. Millions of people are lining up before sunrise, and prices are crashing everywhere.
So why would anyone name a day this exciting — Black Friday?
Most people will tell you it's about money. Stores spend the year in the red, and this is the day their books finally flip into the black.
It's a great story. It just isn't the original one.
Rewind to Philadelphia, in the nineteen fifties and sixties.
Every year, the day after Thanksgiving, shoppers flooded downtown — right before the big Army-Navy football game that Saturday.
Police officers couldn't take the day off — so they gave it a grim nickname: Black Friday.
Store owners hated it. They even tried rebranding it as Big Friday. It didn't stick.
So years later, a happier explanation spread — red ink turning black. By the nineteen eighties, that's the version everyone told.
Today, Black Friday reaches Canada, Britain, and far beyond — and more of it happens on phones than ever.
So the name on every sale banner you'll see today — started as a police complaint.
